messages.content: What are the length and the width of a rectangle which has a perimeter of 14 and area of 15.

message.content:
The two unknowns \(x\) (length) and \(y\) (width) satisfy  

\[
\begin{cases}
2(x+y)=14 \quad &(\text{perimeter})\\[4pt]
xy=15          \quad &(\text{area})
\end{cases}\Longrightarrow 
\begin{cases}
x+y=7 \\[4pt]
xy=15 .
\end{cases}
\]

Treat one side as a variable \(t\). Then the other side is \(7-t\), so

\[
t(7-t)=15 \;\Rightarrow\; 7t-t^{2}=15 \;\Rightarrow\;
t^{2}-7t+15=0 .
\]

This quadratic equation has discriminant  

\[
D = (-7)^2-4\cdot1\cdot15 = 49-60 = -11 < 0 .
\]

Because the discriminant is negative, there are **no real‑valued** solutions for \(x\) and \(y\).

In practical terms this means it’s mathematically impossible for a rectangle with a perimeter of \(14\) units to have an area of \(15\) square units—there simply aren’t positive real numbers whose sum is \(7\) and whose product is \(15\). If you allow complex dimensions, the “solutions” would be

\[
x=\frac{7}{2}+i\,\frac{\sqrt{11}}{2}, \qquad  
y=\frac{7}{2}-i\,\frac{\sqrt{11}}{2},
\]

but such values do not correspond to a physically realizable rectangle.
